summary: Kole Jain looks at 50 landing pages, mostly software sites (the description admits a few are not), and pulls out seven recurring section layouts, then rebuilds each one in a Figma file offered as a free download. The seven are: a customer logo strip, a hero with big text and a big image, a tabbed 'clickable multisection', simple and tasteful hover animations, a 'simple bento' grid, a 'straight line grid' with visible grid lines, and images inside the navigation menu. He names real sites that use each one and gives practical tips, such as a plain or a marquee version of the logo strip, designing every tab before handoff, and keeping bento grids simple so developers can build them. For a design system, the video works as a catalogue of marketing-page section patterns with options that could be offered as visual samples, plus a steady push toward simple, well-built motion over heavy graphics [inferred].
key_ideas: Most software landing pages share the same few section layouts, so the job is to use them well and add a distinctive touch.
Customer logos are the most common section: 41 of the 50 sites showed well-known logos as social proof.
A logo strip can be a simple static row or a marquee that slides the logos across, with a gradient and progressive blur at the edges.
The standard hero is big text, a big image and lots of space, which pulls people into scrolling for more.
When everyone uses the same hero, set yours apart with a distinctive font, an inline diagram, an interactive product image or a subtle background gradient.
A tabbed 'clickable multisection' can switch automatically on a timer or use a simpler layout; whichever you pick, design every tab before handoff.
Software sites are moving away from heavy graphics toward simple, tasteful animations, and those animations have to be done well.
An imported third-party effect can look blurry and give itself away; simple hover effects built with care look better.
A 'simple bento' built on plain grids gives the bento trend without the build cost of an Apple-style bento.
A 'straight line grid' keeps visible grid lines between feature cells instead of floating cards.
Images in the navigation menu give people context at a glance before they click, which beats plain lists of links.
People don't pay attention for long and don't read all the copy, so adding images to the nav makes their life easier.

rules.rule: Consider a customer logo section on a software landing page, using well-recognized logos as social proof.
rules.why: 41 of the 50 sites had one, and visitors automatically assume the logos are important companies that use the product.
rules.evidence: 41 of the 50 softwares I looked at

rules.rule: For a plain logo strip, lay only your most important logos across the screen, without animation.
rules.why: It is the simple way, and the one the presenter likes.
rules.evidence: take your most important logos throw them across the screen

rules.rule: For a fancier logo strip, slide the logos across the screen left to right in a marquee and fade them out at the edges with a gradient plus a progressive blur.
rules.why: The presenter says that if you are getting fancy, and you probably should, this is the version to build.
rules.evidence: the bougie one where we would have a marquee animation

rules.rule: Build the hero with big text, a big image and generous space around them.
rules.why: This makes people start scrolling for more information without realising it.
rules.evidence: big text Big Image lots of space

rules.rule: Give a standard hero a distinctive element, such as a distinctive font, a small inline diagram or an interactive product image.
rules.why: When everyone uses the same layout, you need to be more creative to set yourself apart.
rules.evidence: get a little more creative to differentiate ourselves

rules.rule: Consider a very subtle gradient behind the hero rather than a flat background.
rules.why: Without the gradient the hero becomes more bland and boring.
rules.evidence: I added a very subtle gradient here

rules.rule: When designing a tabbed section (clickable multisection), design the content of every tab before handing off to a developer or client.
rules.why: Otherwise the developer or client receives it with half the site missing.
rules.evidence: make sure to design all the tabs

rules.rule: If you don't want the extra work, use a simpler tabbed layout like MongoDB's instead of automatic switching with a timer like Webflow's.
rules.why: Automatic switching with a timer is more complex; if you don't want to do all of that, a MongoDB-style layout is probably a little better.
rules.evidence: something like mongod DBS layout is probably a little better

rules.rule: Use simple, tasteful animations on software marketing pages instead of heavy, render-intensive graphics.
rules.why: Modern software designs are shifting away from heavy graphics, and software sites typically prefer simple, tasteful animations.
rules.evidence: softwares typically prefer simple and tasteful animations

rules.rule: Don't ship an animation that renders blurry, such as a scroll effect imported from a third party; build each animation cleanly.
rules.why: The blur gives away that it was imported, and the key is to actually do these animations well.

rules.rule: Keep hover effects simple and well built; don't go overboard with them.
rules.why: Simple and well put together is always better.
rules.evidence: don't go overboard don't make it crazy

rules.rule: Build bento sections on simple grids (a 'simple bento') rather than a complex Apple-style bento.
rules.why: Complex bentos are very hard to put together, while simple grids keep developers happy and still follow the trend.
rules.evidence: sticking to some pretty simple grids so our Dev doesn't rip us a new one

rules.rule: Consider one slightly tilted card inside a simple bento.
rules.why: Ramp's bento, the presenter's favourite, does this.
rules.evidence: ramps Bento that has a slightly tilted card

rules.rule: Consider a straight line grid for feature blocks: keep visible grid lines between cells instead of letting them float apart.
rules.why: The presenter sees it more and more, for example on Vercel's six-section block; Qatalog pairs its line grids with tasteful animations.
rules.evidence: what I've termed the straight line grid

rules.rule: Add images to navigation dropdown menus instead of showing only lists of links.
rules.why: People skim and rarely read copy, and images give context about where a link goes at a glance before they click.

rules.rule: Even on a small website, use a small image menu (like Pipe's); most SaaS sites use giant image dropdowns (like Intercom's).
rules.why: Pipe's small image menu looks really professional and works well.
rules.evidence: even if you've got a small website

decisions.question: How should the customer logo strip look?

options.name: Simple static strip
options.effect: Your most important logos laid across the screen, and you're good to go.
options.when: You want the simple way; the presenter's own preference.

options.name: Marquee with edge fade
options.effect: Logos slide across the screen, and a gradient plus progressive blur fades them out at the edges.
options.when: You want a fancier, moving section; the presenter says you probably should.

decisions.recommendation: Both are offered. The presenter likes the simple row but says getting fancy with the marquee is probably worth it.
decisions.evidence: there are two main ways of going about this

decisions.question: How should the page show social proof: customer logos, or a direct comparison with competitors?

options.name: Well-known customer logos
options.effect: Visitors assume important companies use the product.
options.when: The most common choice (41 of 50 sites).

options.name: Competitor call-out through a testimonial
options.effect: A customer quote does the comparing for you.
options.when: You want to position against rivals without saying it yourself (Coda).

options.name: Direct competitor call-out
options.effect: The page openly tells people to drop other tools.
options.when: You want a blunt, confident tone (Basecamp).

decisions.evidence: on the complete other side of social proof

decisions.question: How should the hero be aligned?

options.name: The common hero layout
options.effect: The layout shared by dozens of software sites, with big text, a big image and lots of space; likely centered, since the source contrasts it with left-aligned heroes [inferred]
options.when: You want the familiar, proven structure.

options.name: Left-aligned text
options.effect: Hero text lined up on the left, as on Linear.
options.when: An alternative the presenter left out of his count (Linear); choosing it to stand apart is [inferred].

decisions.recommendation: The source does not choose between them; it explains the common layout as big text, a big image and lots of space, then says to add a distinctive touch.
decisions.evidence: landing pages that had left Al line text like linear

decisions.question: How do you make a standard hero stand out?

options.name: Distinctive font and inline diagram
options.effect: A nifty, characterful typeface and a small inline diagram in the hero.
options.when: You want personality without changing the layout (Magier).

options.name: Interactive product image
options.effect: The full-size hero image responds to the visitor.
options.when: You can invest in interaction (ClickUp).

options.name: Subtle background gradient
options.effect: Removes the bland, flat feel of a plain background.
options.when: When the hero looks flat; the presenter uses it on his own hero.

decisions.recommendation: Get a little creative to set yourself apart, since everyone uses the same layout.
decisions.evidence: get a little more creative to differentiate ourselves

decisions.question: How should a tabbed feature section (clickable multisection) behave?

options.name: Automatic switching with a timer
options.effect: Tabs advance by themselves on a timer.
options.when: You want a more complex, self-running section (Webflow).

options.name: Simpler layout
options.effect: A simpler tabbed section without automatic switching.
options.when: You don't want all that extra work (MongoDB).

options.name: Horizontal or vertical tab layout
options.effect: Horizontal and vertical versions of the section.
options.when: Either works; Miro uses both, four times on one page.

decisions.recommendation: The simpler MongoDB-style layout is probably better if you don't want the extra work, and design every tab either way.
decisions.evidence: some are more complex with automatic switching and a timer

decisions.question: How complex should a bento section be?

options.name: Complex bento (Apple-style)
options.effect: Rich, irregular tiles; very hard to put together.
options.when: Marketing purposes, per the source.

options.name: Simple bento
options.effect: Tiles on plain grids that still read as a bento; easy for developers.
options.when: Software sites (Butter, Kit).

options.name: Simple bento with a tilted card
options.effect: One slightly tilted card breaks the grid for interest.
options.when: You want a little more character (Ramp).

decisions.recommendation: Use a simple bento on simple grids so it can be built, while still following the trend.
decisions.evidence: what I've proclaimed to be the simple Bento

decisions.question: Should feature cells float apart, or sit in a grid with visible lines?

options.name: Floating cells
options.effect: Separate blocks floating apart on the page.
options.when: The approach the line grid replaces.

options.name: Straight line grid
options.effect: Cells share visible grid lines, like Vercel's six-section block or Qatalog.
options.when: You want the structured look the presenter sees more and more, often with tasteful animations.

decisions.evidence: instead of having these floating around we keep these grids in there

decisions.question: What should navigation dropdown menus show?

options.name: Plain lists of links
options.effect: Text only; people don't know where a link goes until they click.
options.when: Not recommended by the source.

options.name: Giant image dropdown
options.effect: A large menu with images, as on Intercom.
options.when: What most SaaS sites have (Intercom).

options.name: Small image menu
options.effect: A compact menu with images that looks professional.
options.when: Even a small website (Pipe).

decisions.recommendation: Add images to the nav: they are more appealing and give context at a glance, and the presenter expects this 2025 trend to stick.

decisions.question: How much visual effect should a software marketing page use?

options.name: Heavy graphics
options.effect: Render-intensive visuals that the presenter mocks as needing an expensive GPU.
options.when: Not recommended by the source.

options.name: Simple, tasteful animations
options.effect: Simple hover effects, done cleanly.
options.when: What software sites typically prefer (Welcome, Pipe, Klaviyo).

decisions.recommendation: Simple, tasteful animations, done well; don't go overboard.
decisions.evidence: modern designs are shifting away from Graphics

process.detail: Look through a large set of comparable sites (here 50 software landing pages) and note which sections keep recurring.
Note how often a section appears (41 of 50 sites had logos) and try to get to the bottom of why these sites look better than your own designs.
Build your own version of each layout (for the logo strip, both a simple and a fancier version) and add a distinctive touch so it doesn't look like everyone else's.
Fill in every tab and section so the developer or client doesn't receive a design with half the site missing.

caveats: Self-promotion: a free Figma file download on the presenter's site, a design challenge with $2k in prizes on newform.community, a plug for his design community, and a pointer to an earlier video where the hero dashboard was designed.
The sample of 50 is personal and informal; the description says it includes a few non-software sites, and the counts (such as 41 of 50) are from that sample only.
Dated: published February 2025 and framed around 2025 design trends.
'Clickable multisection', 'simple bento' and 'straight line grid' are names the presenter made up, not industry terms.
Mostly opinion and observation with humour and some crude language; no exact values (sizes, colors, timings) are given in the transcript, so the visuals are only on screen.

Auto-caption name fixes applied: 'mag'/'magier' is Magier, 'catalog' is Qatalog, and 'better stack' is Better Stack (magier.com, qatalog.com and betterstack.com are in the truncated description); the rest are [inferred]: 'Kota'/'Koda' is Coda, 'versel' is Vercel, 'mongod DBS' is MongoDB, 'mirro'/'Muro' is Miro, 'clavio' is Klaviyo, 'web flow' is Webflow, 'design Joy' is DesignJoy, 'beehive' is beehiiv, 'SAS' is SaaS, 'Beno' is bento. 'welcome' in the animation list is kept as heard. Some names in the long hero list ('siif', 'forell', 'SE steam Juno', 'Loop mail trimp') are unclear and were left out.
The phrase before 'on your competitors' appears to be a censored word in the captions; the section is about openly calling out competitors.
The competitor call-out is a brief aside; the presenter says they are getting sidetracked and moves on to the hero.
